History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old male plastic surgeon with 1.5–2-month history of recurrent, transient right-sided sensory and motor deficits (hand pins-and-needles, arm/leg weakness, abnormal gait) and associated fatigue; increasing in frequency to several episodes per day. No current symptoms. Concern for transient ischaemic attacks (TIA); urgent outpatient stroke/TIA clinic referral arranged.

History:
• Chief complaint: Episodic right-sided pins-and-needles and limb weakness.  
• Symptom onset: ~6–8 weeks ago.  
• Course: Initially once weekly to monthly; now occurring a couple of times per day. Each episode lasts “a few days” then resolves.  
• Sensory symptoms: Pins-and-needles confined to right hand.  
• Motor symptoms: Subjective weakness of right arm and right leg; colleague noticed abnormal gait during episodes. Difficulty holding coffee cup during episodes.  
• Bulbar symptoms: Sensation of “something in my throat” during episodes but denies objective dysphagia; speech unaffected.  
• Visual symptoms: None reported.  
• Constitutional/other: Fatigue and occasional nausea during symptomatic periods; otherwise well.  
• Triggers/relievers: None identified.  
• Systems review (pertinent negatives): No persistent speech disturbance, no vision loss, no persistent swallowing difficulty, no current symptoms at time of consult.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• Prior cardiovascular risk assessment after father’s surgery—cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes screen reportedly normal.

Medications:
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily (self-initiated; dose/route/frequency documented).  
• No other medications noted.

Allergies:
• Penicillin – reaction not specified.

Social History:
• Occupation: Plastic surgeon (medical doctor).  
• Living situation: Lives with wife.  
• Tobacco: Denies smoking.  
• Alcohol/substance use: Not discussed.  
• No other social or financial concerns mentioned.

Family History:
• Father: Carotid surgery performed to reduce stroke risk (suggests carotid stenosis/TIA or stroke history).  
• No other familial illnesses discussed.

Physical Examination:
• No physical examination or vital signs documented (video lost during call).

Investigations:
• None performed during consult.  
• Planned: Carotid Doppler ultrasound and possible brain imaging (CT/MRI) to be arranged by TIA clinic.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Recurrent transient right-sided neurological deficits, ?TIA:  
  • Assessment: Episodes of unilateral sensory and motor deficits with spontaneous resolution; strong suspicion for transient ischaemic attacks given symptom pattern and positive family history.  
  • Plan:  
    – Urgent referral to stroke/TIA clinic; target review within 1–2 days.  
    – Expected tests: carotid duplex, brain imaging, additional vascular/cardiac work-up per protocol.  
    – Provide patient with TIA clinic and PALS contact numbers; advise calling to confirm appointment.  
    – Education: Warned to attend Emergency Department immediately if symptoms recur and are prolonged or do not resolve.  
    – GP to file referral promptly (completed during call).

Issue 2 – Aspirin use without formal indication:  
  • Assessment: Patient self-started aspirin 75 mg daily post father’s surgery; risks/benefits not previously reviewed.  
  • Plan:  
    – Document current use; final decision to continue, adjust, or discontinue to be made after stroke/TIA assessment.  
    – Advise patient on potential risks of aspirin (bleeding) and importance of specialist review.

General plan items:  
• Follow-up: Await stroke/TIA clinic outcome; patient to re-contact GP if appointment delayed or new concerns arise.  
• Safety-netting: Clear return precautions provided for persistent or worsening neurological symptoms.

Quality checks:

Missing but clinically expected elements:
• No vital signs, cardiovascular, or neurological examination documented.  
• No medication reconciliation beyond aspirin.  
• No alcohol history, exercise habits, or detailed cardiovascular risk factors documented.  
• No documentation of reaction type to penicillin allergy.

Internal conflicts:
• None noted.

Transcript quality:
• Occasional audio/video dropouts but overall clinically adequate; physical examination limited by virtual format.
